To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we detected C. burnetius DNA in 11% of the ticks collected from Ethiopian cows.

1) Coxiella burnetiia, the causative agent of Q fever and a zoonosis of worldwide distribution, was identified in Ethiopian cattle ticks, 2) the genetic characterization of these isolates showed that they are closely related to C. burnetiia strains found previously in other regions of the world, 3) the genetic information of these Ethiopian isolates will be helpful for future studies to understand the genetic variability of the agent and its host adaptation

the present study identified novel C. burnetiii genotypes from Ethiopian ticks, that these genotypes are related to previously described ones and that the host specific adaptation of C. burnetiia is confirmed by our findings.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of C. burnetiigenotypes circulating in Ethiopia.
the genetic characterization of a novel Coxiella burnetiigenotype from ticks in Ethiopia and its comparison to previously described genotyping results.
the detection, genetic characterization, and the identification of new genetic variants of C. burnetti in Ethiopia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present C. burnetiu genotypes from East Africa are not different from other genotypes from other parts of the globe, which is in accordance with the presumed host-specificity of this agent.
the C. burnetiis circulating in Ethiopia belong to genotypes that have been described from other countries and are most likely transmitted by cattle.
C. burnetiu genotypes are not host-specific but rather that they have a strong association with a specific source host.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

C. burneti genotypes found in Ethiopian ticks are highly related to the ones detected in other parts of world and that these are likely acquired from cattle, which are also the source hosts of these ticks.
the Ethiopian C. burnetiii isolates are genetically related to isolates from cattle from other parts of the globe and are genetically distinct from isolates from humans.
C. burnetius genotypes circulating in Ethiopia are closely related to those found in other parts of Africa as well as other continents.
The main takeaway from our work is that
C. burnetius genotypes from Ethiopia are closely related to those from other parts of the globe, which suggests that this agent is globally distributed and may have adapted to a wide range of hosts.
C. burnetius is widely present and diverse in the Ethiopian cattle and tick populations.
the C. burneti strains circulating in Ethiopia belong to the same clade with strains circulating elsewhere in the world.
